original_text: Virus Overview¨Viruses related to a variety of plant, animal, and human disease. ¨Non-cellular construction¨May have DNA or RNA genome¨Able to evolve as a result of mutations¨Require the machinery of the host cell they infect to replicate ¨Not considered living¤Do not have metabolism, cannot respond to stimuli
explanation: Viruses are infectious agents associated with a wide variety of diseases in plants, animals, and humans. They feature a non-cellular construction and can possess either a DNA or RNA genome. Because they can acquire mutations, they are able to evolve. However, they are not considered living organisms because they do not have a metabolism and cannot respond to environmental stimuli. To replicate, they must infect a host cell and exploit its cellular machinery.

explanation: Louis Pasteur was among the first to hypothesize the existence of infectious agents smaller than bacteria, which was later confirmed in the mid-20th century via electron microscopy. Classification of viruses consists of two parts. The first part categorizes viruses into Groups I through IV based on genome structure (DNA vs RNA, single vs double stranded). The second part uses a hierarchy similar to Linnaean classification (Order, Family, Genus, and Species) but does not include any taxonomic ranks higher than Order. For example, chickenpox is classified as Varicellovirus Zoster, and the seasonal flu is an example of a new strain that develops within a single viral species annually.

explanation: Viruses range in size from 10 to 400 nm. They are categorized based on three criteria: shape, genetic material, and the presence or absence of an outer envelope. All viruses possess a common basic anatomy consisting of an outer protein capsid (made of protein complexes) and an inner core of nucleic acid, which contains between 3 to hundreds of genes. Viruses that lack an outer envelope are termed 'naked' viruses. Enveloped viruses feature an outer coating made of cell plasma membrane acquired from the host cell.

original_text: Virus Reproduction¨Technically intracellular parasites –Do not contain their own machinery for reproduction¨Gain entry into specific host cell ¤Capsid (or spikes of the envelope) adhere to specific receptor sites on the host cell surface. ¨Viral nucleic acid then enters a cell ¤Viral genome codes for production of protein units in the capsid. explanation: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites because they lack their own machinery for reproduction. To replicate, they must enter a specific host cell. This entry is initiated when the viral capsid or the spikes of its envelope adhere to specific receptor sites on the host cell surface. After attachment, the viral nucleic acid enters the host cell. The viral genome then directs the host cell to synthesize capsid protein subunits, which assemble into new viral particles. In this process, the virus relies completely on the host cell's enzymes, ribosomes, transfer RNA (tRNA), and ATP. Mistakes made during viral genome replication introduce mutations, which can lead to viral evolution.

explanation: Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that infect bacterial cells. Viruses replicate using two main types of life cycles: the lytic cycle and the lysogenic cycle. In the lytic cycle, the virus infects the cell, takes control of the host machinery to synthesize new viruses, and bursts the host cell open to release them. The lytic cycle proceeds through five distinct stages: Attachment, Penetration, Biosynthesis, Maturation, and Release. The Ebola virus behaves via a lytic cycle. In the lysogenic cycle, the virus infects the cell but integrates its genetic material into the host genome (integration occurs after penetration). There is no immediate viral proliferation, and the virus can remain dormant for years before potentially entering the lytic cycle. HIV is an example of a lysogenic virus that remains dormant before replicating.

explanation: When animal viruses infect a cell, they undergo an uncoating process that releases their viral DNA or RNA. The method of viral release depends on the presence of an envelope. Naked viruses (lacking an envelope) typically release new particles by bursting (lysing) the host cell. Enveloped viruses exit via budding: the viral particles migrate to the host cell membrane, form a bud, and exit, wrapping themselves in a portion of the host cell's membrane that has been modified with viral proteins and carbohydrates. Retroviruses are RNA viruses that possess the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which transcribes viral RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA). This cDNA integrates into the host cell's genome and replicates alongside it. The viral DNA is later transcribed to produce new viral particles. HIV and Human T Lymphotropic Virus 1 are examples of retroviruses.

explanation: Emerging viruses are viruses that have recently crossed species barriers or have infected previously unaffected populations, such as H1N1 flu, West Nile virus, and COVID-19. In influenza pandemics, the viral structure features two critical surface proteins: the H (hemagglutinin) spike and the N (neuraminidase) spike. The H spike, which has 16 different types, binds to receptors on host cell membranes. The N spike, which has 9 different types, attacks host cell membranes to facilitate the exit of mature viruses. Because each type of spike has multiple varieties, the host's immune system can only recognize and defend against H and N spikes to which it has previously been exposed.

explanation: Viroids and prions are sub-viral infectious particles. Viroids consist of naked strands of RNA with no surrounding capsid. They are associated with several crop diseases, instructing host plant cells to replicate more viroids. Prions, or proteinaceous infectious particles, are abnormal proteins. They share a similar primary sequence with normal cellular proteins but possess a different, contagious tertiary conformation. When prions interact with normal proteins, they force them to adopt the abnormal conformation at an exponential rate. Prions cause neurodegenerative diseases known as Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathies (TSEs). A notable example is Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE, or Mad Cow disease), which occurs in cattle and can be transmitted to humans.

explanation: Prokaryotes comprise two major groups: bacteria and archaea, both of which are fully functioning cells. They are incredibly abundant; for instance, a single spoonful of soil can contain more than 1,000 prokaryotic cells. Structurally, they are very small, typically ranging in size from 1 to 10 micrometers (μm) in length and 0.7 to 1.5 μm in width. Historically, it was believed that prokaryotic organisms could spontaneously generate from non-living matter, a concept that was successfully disproved in the 1850s by Louis Pasteur.

original_text: Structure¨Lack a membrane-bounded nucleus (DNA in nucleoid region) ¨Outer cell wall containing peptidoglycan ¨Some move by means of flagella ¨Lack membranous organelles ¨May have accessory ring of DNA (plasmid)
explanation: Prokaryotic cells have distinct structural characteristics. First, they lack a membrane-bounded nucleus, meaning their DNA is localized in a region known as the nucleoid. Second, they have a protective outer cell wall that contains peptidoglycan. Third, some prokaryotes are motile and achieve movement via flagella. Fourth, they lack membranous organelles. Finally, many prokaryotes carry an accessory ring of DNA called a plasmid, which is separate from their main chromosomal DNA.

explanation: Prokaryotes reproduce asexually via a process called binary fission. To introduce genetic variety, prokaryotes employ methods of genetic recombination. The three main methods are conjugation, transformation, and transduction. In conjugation, a physical connection called a sex pilus forms between two prokaryotic cells. The donor cell then passes a copy of its DNA to the recipient cell through this pilus.

explanation: Two other major methods of genetic recombination in prokaryotes are transformation and transduction. Transformation occurs when a bacterial cell absorbs free pieces of foreign DNA from its environment (released by other prokaryotes) and incorporates them into its own genome. Transduction, on the other hand, is mediated by viruses. It occurs when bacteriophages, serving as vectors, transport fragments of bacterial DNA from a previously infected host cell into a new bacterial host cell.

explanation: Prokaryotes have different relationships with oxygen. They can be divided into three categories based on oxygen requirements: 1) Obligate aerobes, which cannot survive or grow without free oxygen; 2) Obligate anaerobes, which cannot grow in the presence of free oxygen and are harmed by it; and 3) Facultative anaerobes, which are metabolic generalists able to grow in either the presence or the absence of free oxygen.

explanation: Prokaryotes show incredibly diverse nutritional strategies. Photoautotrophs are photosynthetic organisms that capture solar energy to reduce carbon dioxide to organic compounds. Chemoautotrophs are chemosynthetic organisms that oxidize inorganic compounds to acquire energy, which is then used to reduce CO2 to an organic compound. The majority of prokaryotes, however, are chemoheterotrophs that consume pre-formed organic nutrients. Within this group, aerobic saprotrophs decompose large organic molecules into smaller, reusable molecules, making them critical components of healthy ecosystems. Furthermore, prokaryotes can be free-living or engage in symbiotic relationships, including nitrogen fixation (mutualistic relationships), commensalism, and parasitism.

explanation: Domain Bacteria contains the more common types of prokaryotes, with over 2,000 species named. Most bacteria are surrounded by a protective cell wall containing peptidoglycan. The Gram stain procedure is commonly used for diagnosing and classifying bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria retain the primary dye and appear purple after washing, while Gram-negative bacteria lose the dye and appear pink. Bacteria are also classified based on three physical shapes: spiral (spirilli), rod-shaped (bacilli), and round (cocci).

Cyanobacteria lack any visible means of locomotion and are able to survive in extreme environments. When they form commensal relationships with fungi, they form lichens.

original_text: Domain Archaea¨Archaea were earlier considered bacteria ¤Discovered that the base sequence of their rRNA differs from Bacteria ¤Other differences: nArchaea do not have peptidoglycan in their cell walls like the Bacteria nArchaea biochemical more like Eukarya than BacterianArchaea now thought to be more closely related to Eukarya than to Bacteria¨Most are chemoautotrophs ¨Some mutualistic, Some commensalistic¨None known to be parasitic ¨None are photosynthetic
explanation: Archaea were once classified as bacteria, but scientists discovered that their ribosomal RNA (rRNA) base sequences differ from those of bacteria. Other key differences include: Archaea cell walls lack peptidoglycan, and their biochemistry is more similar to Eukarya than to Bacteria. Thus, Archaea are now considered more closely related to Eukarya than to Bacteria. Most Archaea are chemoautotrophs. They can form mutualistic or commensalistic relationships, but none are known to be parasitic, and none are photosynthetic.

Archaea ribosomal RNA base sequences differ from Bacteria, and their cell walls lack peptidoglycan.

explanation: Protists are the simplest yet most biologically diverse eukaryotes, primarily inhabiting marine or freshwater environments. Most protists are unicellular, but some are colonial (like Volvox) or multicellular (like Kelp, a brown algae that can grow up to 200m). Spirogyra is a unicellular filamentous example. Protists possess membrane-bound organelles, such as mitochondria. They reproduce primarily asexually, but under certain conditions, they can reproduce sexually by producing spores that remain dormant until conditions are favorable. Their nutrition varies widely: photoautotrophs contain chloroplasts; heterotrophs absorb organic molecules or ingest food particles; and mixotrophs combine photosynthesis and heterotrophic nutrition. While many protists cause human disease, they are critical ecological components.

explanation: Protists were historically classified under a single kingdom because they were thought to be monophyletic. However, DNA evidence has shown that all protists do not evolve from a single common ancestor, revealing instead six distinct evolutionary lines. Eukaryotes, including protists, are therefore grouped into Supergroups, which represent taxonomic levels below domain but above kingdom, each representing a separate evolutionary lineage. The six supergroups are Archaeplastida, Chromalveolata, Excavata, Amoebozoa (Amoebazoan), Opisthokonta (Opisthokontan), and Rhizaria.

explanation: Supergroup Excavata includes animal-like zooflagellates characterized by atypical or absent mitochondria and distinctive flagella and/or deep, excavated oral grooves. explanation: Supergroup Amoebozoa (Amoebazoa) includes protozoans that move using pseudopods (false-feet). explanation: Most fungi are multicellular. Multicellular fungi possess a thallus or body structure called a mycelium, which is made of a network of filaments known as hyphae. Fungi lack chloroplasts and have cell walls composed of chitin rather than cellulose. They are non-motile, meaning their only movement is the growth extension of their hyphae toward a food source.

explanation: Fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually. Fungal sexual reproduction involves three stages: 1) Haploid Hyphae, 2) Dikaryotic Stage, in which hyphae from two different mating types fuse, leaving paired, unfused haploid nuclei, and 3) Diploid Zygote, where nuclear fusion creates a diploid nucleus. Some species reproduce only asexually through windblown spores, and unicellular yeast reproduce asexually by budding.

explanation: Phylum Ascomycota, also called Sac Fungi, contains around 50,000 species, most of which are saprotrophs with septate hyphae. original_text: Diversity -Ascomycota¨Sexual reproduction¤Ascusis a fingerlike sac that develops during sexualnMay be surrounded and protected by sterile hyphae within a fruiting body called an ascocarpnIn cup fungi, ascocarpare cup shapednIn morels, they are stalked and crowned by a pitted bell-shapednHaploid hyphae fuse to make diploidnMeiosis occurs, followed by mitosis –results in 8 ascosporesnSpores move by wind, contact female organ, and produce new haploid hyphae
explanation: During Ascomycota sexual reproduction, a specialized fingerlike sac called an ascus is formed. These asci are often protected by a surrounding layer of sterile hyphae within a fruiting body called an ascocarp. The shape of the ascocarp varies: it is cup-shaped in cup fungi and stalked with a pitted bell-shaped crown in morels. The reproduction process involves the fusion of haploid hyphae to form a diploid nucleus, which undergoes meiosis followed by a single mitotic division, resulting in 8 haploid ascospores. These spores are dispersed by the wind, and upon contacting a female organ, they germinate to produce new haploid hyphae.

original_text: Ascomycota –Benefits and Harms¨Yeast¤Used to make beer and wine, bread leavening¤Genetic experiments –model organism¤Candida albicanscauses fungal infections –oral thrush¨Molds¤Aspergillus–green molds used to produce soy sauce, and citric and gallic acids¤Aspergillus flavus secretes a carcinogenic toxin¤Trichophyton–athletes foot¤Histoplasma capsulatum leads to “fungal flu”¨Mushrooms¤Yummy¤Certain wild varieties poisonousnRed and yellow AmanitasnDeath angel mushroom, Amanita phalloides, 90% of fatalities from wild mushroomsnAbdominal pain, vomiting, hallucinationsnPoison inhibits RNA polymerase, leading to kidney andliver damage
explanation: Ascomycota and other fungi exhibit a wide array of benefits and harms. Yeasts are widely utilized in making beer, wine, and bread, and serve as model organisms in genetic research, but Candida albicans causes infections like oral thrush. Molds such as Aspergillus are used to produce soy sauce, citric acid, and gallic acid. However, Aspergillus flavus secretes a carcinogenic toxin, Trichophyton causes athlete's foot, and Histoplasma capsulatum causes 'fungal flu'. Regarding mushrooms, while many are edible, some are extremely poisonous. Wild varieties like the red and yellow Amanitas, specifically the Death Angel mushroom (Amanita phalloides), cause 90% of wild mushroom fatalities. This toxin inhibits RNA polymerase, leading to abdominal pain, vomiting, hallucinations, and severe kidney and liver damage.

explanation: Phylum Basidiomycota, known as Club Fungi, comprises around 22,000 species, including toadstools, mushrooms, bracket fungi, and puffballs. Some species are poisonous, and some cause plant diseases like smuts and rusts. The mycelium of Basidiomycota has septate hyphae. They typically reproduce sexually. Haploid hyphae fuse to form a dikaryotic mycelium (n + n), which develops into a fruiting body called a basidiocarp. This fruiting body contains club-shaped reproductive structures called basidia. Within the basidium, nuclear fusion is followed by meiosis to produce basidiospores.

original_text: Symbiotic Relationships of Fungi¨Lichen¤Fungus & Cyanobacterium or green algaenFungal hyphae penetrates photosynthetic symbiontnNutrients transferred to fungusnPossibly mutualistic but fungus more parasiticnPhotosynthetic symbiont independentnFungal symbiont cannot grow alone¤3 morphological typesnCompact crustose –found on bare rocks or tree barknFruticose –shrublikenFoliose –leaflike¤Can live in extreme conditions¤Sensitive indicators of air pollution¨Mycorrhizae¤Discussed earlier
explanation: Lichens represent a symbiotic relationship between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, which can be either a cyanobacterium or green algae. Fungal hyphae penetrate the photosynthetic host cell to transfer nutrients back to the fungus. Although historically considered mutualistic, the relationship may be more parasitic because the photosynthetic partner can live independently, whereas the fungal partner cannot grow alone. Lichens exhibit three morphological growth forms: 1) compact crustose (often found on bare rocks or tree bark), 2) fruticose (shrublike), and 3) foliose (leaflike). Lichens are highly resilient, allowing them to live in extreme environments, but they are also highly sensitive indicators of air pollution. Mycorrhizae are another major symbiotic relationship of fungi, as discussed previously.

explanation: Plants are multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryotes that adapted to a terrestrial lifestyle. RNA analysis suggests that plants evolved from green algae, with Charophytes being their closest relative. Adapting to land required plants to overcome the threat of desiccation (drying out); however, a significant advantage of land was that carbon dioxide (CO2) was much more available in the air. Plants store excess carbohydrates as starch and have cell walls made of cellulose.

original_text: Alternation of Generations¨Plants go through alternating generations of life¤2n stage and 1n stage¤Spore is the 1n cell created by meiosis.nResults in gametophyte stage, which produces gametes¤Gametes fuse to make 2n zygote which grows through mitosisnResults in sporophyte stage, which will produce spores¤As plants became better adapted to life on land, the sporophyte stage became the dominant cycle
explanation: Plants exhibit an alternation of generations, cycling between diploid (2n) and haploid (1n) stages. The haploid spore is created by meiosis and germinates into the gametophyte stage, which produces gametes. When these gametes fuse, they form a diploid (2n) zygote that grows through mitosis into the sporophyte stage. The sporophyte then produces spores to repeat the cycle. As plants became better adapted to life on land, the sporophyte stage became the dominant phase of their life cycle.

original_text: Common Traits¨Common reproductive traits¤Observed in alternating generations on last slidenEmbryophytaàSporophyte (Sporangia produce spores) àGametophyte (gametangia produce gametes)nMale gametangia = antheridium, female = archegonium¤Common traits associated with land adaptationnExposed parts of plants covered with waxy coatingnCuticle -prevents loss of waternLand plants have little openings for gas exchangenStomata (plural) / Stoma (singular)nPresence of apical tissue –allows ability to produce complex tissue and organs
explanation: Land plants (Embryophytes) share common reproductive and structural traits. Reproductive organs include sporangia on the sporophyte (which produce spores) and gametangia on the gametophyte (which produce gametes). The male gametangium is called the antheridium, and the female is the archegonium. Key adaptations to land life include: 1) a waxy coating called a cuticle covering exposed parts to prevent water loss; 2) microscopic openings called stomata (singular: stoma) that facilitate gas exchange; and 3) the presence of apical tissue, which allows plants to grow and differentiate complex tissues and organs.

original_text: Diversity -Bryophytes¨Nonvascular plants -Liverworts, Hornworts, & Mosses¤Lack specialized means of transporting water and organic nutrients nDo not have true roots, stems, and leaves nMost use Rhyzoidstructure for anchoring¤Only land plant where gametophyte is dominant generationnProduces eggs in archegonia nProduces flagellated sperm in antheridia nSperm swim to egg in film of water to make zygote
explanation: Bryophytes are nonvascular land plants, comprising liverworts, hornworts, and mosses. Because they lack vascular tissue to transport water and organic nutrients, they do not possess true roots, stems, or leaves, instead relying on rhizoid (rhyzoid) structures for anchoring. Bryophytes are the only land plants in which the gametophyte is the dominant generation. The gametophyte produces eggs in archegonia and flagellated sperm in antheridia. The sperm must swim to the egg through a film of environmental water to fertilize it and form the zygote.

original_text: Evolution of Vascular Plants¨Vascular Plants –Have roots that absorb water and nutrients from soil, and transport through a network of tubes¤Xylemconducts water and dissolved minerals up from roots ¤Phloemconducts sucrose and other organic compounds throughout the plant ¤Ligninstrengthens walls of conducting cells in xylem ¤Most seedless vascular plants are homosporousnWindblown spores are dispersal agents ¤All seed plants are heterosporousand have male and female gametophytes nSeeds disperse offspring
explanation: Vascular plants possess roots that absorb water and nutrients from the soil, transporting them through a network of specialized tubes. The vascular tissue includes: 1) Xylem, which conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots, and features walls reinforced with lignin to strengthen the conducting cells; and 2) Phloem, which conducts sucrose and other organic compounds throughout the plant. Most seedless vascular plants are homosporous, producing a single type of spore that acts as a windblown dispersal agent. In contrast, all seed plants are heterosporous, having distinct male and female gametophytes, and they use seeds to disperse their offspring.

Lycophytes possess leaves called microphylls, which contain only a single strand of vascular tissue; this group includes club mosses, ground pines, spike mosses, and quillworts. explanation: Seed plants are the most plentiful plants in the biosphere. A protective seed coat and stored food within the seed allow the plant embryo to survive harsh environmental conditions during extended dormancy. Seed plants are heterosporous, featuring drought-resistant pollen grains and ovules that develop into seeds. Seed plants are categorized into two groups: Gymnosperms (non-flowering plants) and Angiosperms (flowering plants).

explanation: Gymnosperms are seed plants whose seeds are not enclosed by fruit, earning them the term 'naked' seeds. They are divided into 4 groups: 1) Conifers, which produce cones, are monoecious (monecious - both male and female reproductive structures on the same plant), and include pines and redwoods; 2) Cycads, which are tropical plants used in landscaping that tend to be pollinated by insects rather than wind; 3) Ginkgoes, which were dominant in the fossil record but are now represented by only one surviving species, Ginkgo biloba (which is dioecious, meaning individual plants are either male or female); and 4) Gnetophytes, which contain 3 living genera and 70 species, exhibiting varied appearances depending on their location.

explanation: Angiosperms, belonging to the phylum Anthophyta, are an exceptionally large and successful group of plants whose ovules are always enclosed within diploid maternal tissues. They became the dominant plant group during the late Cretaceous and early Paleocene periods. Flowering plants are divided into two classes: 1) Monocots (Monocotyledones), which have one cotyledon in the seed (including corn, tulips, pineapples, bamboo, and sugarcane); and 2) Eudicots (Eudicotyledones or Dicots), which have two cotyledons in the seed (including cacti, strawberries, dandelions, poplars, and beans).

original_text: Angiosperms -The Flower¨Penducle(flower stalk) expands at tip into receptacle¤Bears sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels, all attached to receptacle in whorls¤Calyx (collection of sepals) protect flower bud before it opens¤Corolla (Collection of petals)¨Each stamen consist of an anther and a filament (stalk)¨Carpel has three major regions¤Ovary –Swollen base (fruit)¤Style –elevates stigma¤Stigma –Stick receptor of pollen grains¨Wind-pollinated flowers are usually not showy ¨Bird-pollinated flowers are often colorful ¨Night-blooming flowers attract nocturnal mammals or insects ¤Usually white or cream-colored¨Fruits of flowers protect and aid in dispersal ¤Utilize wind, gravity, water, and animals for dispersal
explanation: The flower develops on a peduncle (flower stalk), which expands at its tip to form the receptacle. The receptacle bears sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels attached in whorls. The calyx is the collection of sepals that protects the bud before opening, and the corolla is the collection of petals. The stamen consists of an anther and a filament stalk. The female carpel has three regions: the swollen ovary base (which becomes the fruit), the style, and the sticky stigma receptor for pollen. Flower appearance is linked to pollination: wind-pollinated flowers are not showy; bird-pollinated flowers are colorful; and night-blooming flowers are typically white or cream-colored to attract nocturnal animals. Fruits protect seeds and aid in their dispersal via wind, gravity, water, and animals.

original_text: Characteristics of Animals¨All animals have a number of common features¤Heterotrophs, that must ingest food, and digest internally¤Cells lack cell walls¤Generally mobile¤Coordinated movement using nerves and muscles¤Reproduce sexuallynInvertebratesnDo not have a backbonenVertebratesnHave a spinal cord or backbone at some stage of their life running down the center of their back¤Most likely descended from an ancestral flagellate colony, where cells took specialized roles¤Wide diversity in body plans, but most members have varying developmental plans controlled by Hoxgene family
explanation: All animals share a set of common features: they are heterotrophs that ingest food and digest it internally; their cells lack cell walls; they are generally mobile; they coordinate movement using nerves and muscles; and they reproduce sexually. Animals are divided into invertebrates (which do not have a backbone) and vertebrates (which have a spinal cord or backbone at some stage of their life running down the center of their back). Animals most likely descended from an ancestral flagellate colony in which cells took on specialized roles. Despite a wide diversity of body plans, most animal developmental pathways are controlled by the Hox gene family.

explanation: Major branches in the animal phylogenetic tree are established based on: 1) Symmetry: radial (organized around a central axis like a wheel) or bilateral (divided into left and right halves along a single longitudinal line); 2) Embryonic Development, specifically tissue layer number: diploblastic organisms have 2 tissue layers (tissues are developed but specialized organs are absent), whereas triploblastic organisms have 3 germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm); and 3) Gastrulation patterns: organisms are either protostomes (mouth develops before the anus) or deuterostomes (anus develops before the mouth). Cleavage of cells, blastula formation, and coelom development also differentiate protostomes and deuterostomes.

explanation: This slide covers simple invertebrates and Radiata. Sponges are the only animals that lack true tissue; they are filter feeders with porous bodies, interior canals lined with flagellated cells, and structural spicules used for species identification. Sponges reproduce both sexually and asexually. Comb Jellies are solitary, free-swimming marine animals (a few cm to 1.5 m long) that move using beating cilia; their body is made of transparent mesoglea, they lack stinging properties (adhering to prey instead), and some are bioluminescent. Cnidarians have stinging cells called cnidocytes, and a body structured as a two-layered sac (the internal digestive cavity also acts as a hydrostatic skeleton). Their body forms are polyp (cup facing up) or medusa (cup facing down), and examples include sea anemone, coral, hydrozoans, jellyfish, and hydra.

explanation: Lophotrochozoans are bilaterally symmetrical at some point in their life and are divided into Lophophorans and Trochozoans. Lophophorans are aquatic animals whose mouth is surrounded by a ciliated, tentacle-like feeding structure called a lophophore (includes Bryozoans, Brachiopods, and Phoronoids). Trochozoans include: 1) Flatworms (Platyhelminthes), which can be free-living planarians (featuring a well-developed excretory system, hermaphroditic sexual reproduction, and a ladder-type nervous system) or parasitic flukes and tapeworms that rely on host systems; and 2) Rotifers (Rotifera), which have a distinctive crown of cilia on their heads.

explanation: Chordates are deuterostomes characterized by an internal bone and cartilage skeleton instead of an exoskeleton. All chordates possess four basic characteristics at some point in their life: 1) a Notochord, which is a dorsal supporting rod that turns into the vertebral column in many chordates; 2) a Dorsal tubular nerve cord, whose anterior portion becomes the brain, and which is known as the spinal cord in many species; 3) Pharyngeal pouches, which are observable in the embryos of most chordates, developing into functional gills in fish and having varying functions in others; and 4) a Postanal tail, which is a tail structure present at some developmental point.

explanation: Vertebrates possess the same 4 chordate characteristics as nonvertebrates in their embryonic stages, but additionally share: 1) a Vertebral column that replaces the embryonic notochord; 2) a Skull enclosing the brain and sensory organs; 3) an Endoskeleton of living tissue that grows with the organism, protecting organs and anchoring muscles; and 4) complex Internal organs (large coelom, complete digestive tract, closed circulatory system, lungs or gills, and separate sexes reproducing sexually). Evolutionarily, vertebrates began with jawless fish, followed by jawed fish. Amphibians were the first terrestrial organisms with limbs, reproducing in water. Reptiles were the first to fully adapt to land, developing amniotic eggs and watertight skin. Birds and mammals evolved further from reptilian lineages.

explanation: Fish represent the largest vertebrate group, ranging from a few millimeters to 12 meters in length. Jawless Fish (Agnathans) are cylindrical (up to a meter long), have smooth, non-scaly skin, act as scavengers feeding on dead fish, and include lampreys. Fish with jaws are ectotherms (body temperature regulated by the environment), and possess gills, a bony endoskeleton, and scales (including extinct placoderms). Cartilaginous fish possess a cartilage skeleton instead of bone, 5-7 open gill slits (no gill cover), teethlike scales, and include sharks, rays, skates, and chimaeras.

Lobe-finned fish contain fleshy fins supported by internal bones. Lobe-finned fish gave rise to the first terrestrial amphibians, and living representatives include the lungfish and coelacanth.

explanation: Amphibians live on both land and water, sharing several unifying characteristics: 1) Limbs: normally tetrapods (having 4 limbs); 2) Smooth, non-scaly skin: adapted for maintaining water balance; 3) Lungs: if present, they are small and used for gas exchange; 4) Double-looped circulatory pathway, featuring a 3-chambered heart; 5) terrestrial-adapted sense organs (sight, hearing, smell); and 6) Ectothermy (body temperature dependent on the environment). Amphibians rely on aquatic reproduction, depositing jelly-coated eggs in water where they are fertilized. The young hatch and grow in water before emerging as terrestrial adults. Amphibian diversity includes salamanders and newts, frogs and toads, and caecilians.

explanation: Reptiles are terrestrial animals (which taxonomically includes birds in class Reptilia) that share several unifying characteristics: 1) Paired limbs: 2 pairs, typically with 5 toes each, adapted for climbing, running, paddling, or flying; 2) Skin: thick, dry, scaly, and impermeable to water; 3) Efficient breathing: lungs are better developed than in amphibians; 4) Efficient circulation: the heart prevents the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood; 5) Efficient excretion: well-developed kidneys; 6) Ectothermy; and 7) Reproduction: internal fertilization and production of amniotic eggs. explanation: Reptile lineages are classified based on the presence and number of openings (temporal fenestrae) behind the eye socket: 1) Anapsid (no opening) - turtles; 2) Diapsid (2 openings) - most reptiles and birds; and 3) Synapsid (1 opening) - mammals. Because most reptiles do not share a single unique common ancestor, Reptilia is considered a paraphyletic group rather than a monophyletic one. Crocodiles and birds are more closely related to dinosaurs than they are to lizards.

explanation: Living reptiles include tortoises and turtles, lizards, snakes, tuataras, and crocodilians. Birds are also included in the reptile lineage and possess characteristic features: 1) feathers, 2) a modified skeleton for flight, 3) modified respiration using lobular lungs, 4) endothermy (using metabolic heat to maintain a constant body temperature), and 5) well-developed sense organs and nervous systems. Bird diversity includes flying birds (e.g., eagles, geese, mockingbirds) and flightless birds (e.g., emu, kiwi, penguin, ostrich). Birds are normally classified by their beak type, foot type, and habitat.

explanation: Mammals share unifying characteristics: hair (ornamental or functional), mammary glands, a skeleton housing a larger brain than reptiles, efficient respiration and circulation with a 4-chambered heart, a developed nervous system, and internal development where offspring are born alive. Mammals are classified into three groups based on offspring birth state: 1) Monotremes (egg-laying mammals) - only includes the duck-billed platypus and Echidna; 2) Marsupials (pouched mammals), whose embryos are nourished by a yolk-based placenta in a pouch (kangaroos, koalas, wombats, opossums); and 3) Placental mammals, which feature an internal placenta for full embryonic growth and development (all other mammals).
